children: The Bank of England was right to keep interest rates unchanged, says David Rees at Schroders in a note. A hike in the autumn now looks more likely, but economic conditions aren't calling for higher rates, he says. "The markets may be building a case for an autumn hike, particularly if other central banks are tightening, but monetary policy should be guided by the fundamentals of the U.K. economy rather than global optics," Rees says. Domestic price growth looks contained, wage growth is slowing and unemployment remains high. "This is not an economy crying out for higher rates," he says. The bigger risk is fiscal policy, Rees says, noting that higher spending could boost domestic inflation and prompt rate hikes. (don.forbes@wsj.com)
